title: A YES on the PAR-Q+ and tightness on the stairs

client.name: Marcus Hale, 52
client.presentation: {not isNull(worseAt) and isNull(emsAt) ? "Pale and sweating, a hand on his chest." : exercising ? "On the step, breathing hard." : not isNull(referredAt) ? "Disappointed but listening; he takes the form." : "Keen to start: his daughter's wedding is in four months."}

readings.label: Chest
readings.value: {not isNull(worseAt) and isNull(emsAt) ? "pain spreading to left arm, sweating" : exercising and not isNull(symptomOnAt) ? "tightness" : "none now"}
readings.flag: (not isNull(worseAt) and isNull(emsAt)) or (exercising and not isNull(symptomOnAt))

items.question: 1. Has a doctor ever said you have a heart condition or high blood pressure?
items.answer: YES: high blood pressure, found two years ago.

items.question: 2. Chest pain at rest, in daily activities, or during physical activity?
items.answer: {isNull(symptomAskedAt) ? "NO" : "NO on paper. In person: tightness on the stairs, which he did not call pain. The honest answer is YES."}

items.question: 3. Dizziness or loss of consciousness in the last 12 months?
5. Prescribed medication for a chronic condition?
items.answer: YES: one blood pressure tablet a day.

items.question: 6. A bone, joint or soft tissue problem that activity could make worse?
7. Told to do only medically supervised activity?
Follow-up questions for his YES answers (pages 2-3)
items.answer: All NO as he answers them: his blood pressure is followed by his doctor and he takes the tablet daily.

findings.label: Current activity
findings.result: No regular exercise for three years; walks the dog 15 minutes most evenings, slowly.

findings.label: What he notices on exertion
findings.result: For about a month, a tightness in the middle of his chest climbing the two flights to his office; it eases within a few minutes of stopping. He has not told his doctor: 'It's just me being out of shape.'

findings.label: Resting measures
findings.result: Seated after five minutes: heart rate 78/min, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg (recorded, not interpreted).

findings.label: Static posture
findings.result: Rounded shoulders and a forward head; feet and knees neutral.

findings.label: During exercise
findings.result: {not isNull(worseAt) ? "The tightness spread to his left arm with sweating and did not ease with rest." : not isNull(resolvedAt) ? "Chest tightness at about three minutes; eased after rest." : not isNull(symptomOnAt) ? "Chest tightness at about three minutes." : "No symptoms so far."}

items.label: Medical clearance first: his doctor, with the PAR-Q+ and a note of the chest tightness
Goals and a schedule agreed for after clearance; no new exercise until then

journal.text: 911 called; front desk sent to meet the crew.

rules.label: PAR-Q+ YES answers
rules.text: Any YES: the follow-up questions, then the ePARmed-X+ or a doctor before a fitness appraisal if any follow-up answer is YES.

rules.label: New sign or symptom, not regularly active
rules.text: Medical clearance before starting (ACSM). No fitness testing or training until then.

rules.label: Warning sign during exercise
rules.text: Stop now and have him rest; chest discomfort is a reason to call 911.
rules.met: (exercising and not isNull(symptomOnAt)) or (not isNull(symptomOnAt) and isNull(calledAt) and isNull(closedAt))

rules.label: Scope of practice
rules.text: Record what he reports; do not diagnose, reassure or interpret a reading as safe.

objective: Preparticipation screening, health history and when to refer to a medical professional
secondaryObjectives: Scope of practice and when to refer to other health professionals
Legal and risk-management basics: liability, documentation, emergency response

sources.cite: NASM Candidate Handbook (updated 9/2025), Appendix A, CPT 7 exam blueprint: Assessment 16% (preparticipation screening, health history and referral), Professional Development and Responsibility 10% (scope of practice, referral, emergency response)
sources.note: Read for the course on 2026-10-08 (backend/supabase/seed/tracks/fitness.ts); not re-read for this case. The objective titles are the course's own words.

sources.cite: PAR-Q+ Collaboration, The Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire for Everyone (PAR-Q+), form dated 01-11-2024, copyright 2025
sources.note: Relevant text: seven general health questions (1 heart condition or high blood pressure; 2 chest pain at rest, in daily activities or during physical activity; 3 dizziness or loss of consciousness in 12 months; 4 another chronic condition; 5 prescribed medication for a chronic condition; 6 a bone, joint or soft tissue problem made worse by activity; 7 told to do only medically supervised activity). Any YES: complete the follow-up questions on pages 2-3; any YES there: 'seek further information before becoming more physically active or engaging in a fitness appraisal', through the ePARmed-X+ and/or a qualified exercise professional. Delay becoming more active if your health changes. 'If in doubt after completing the questionnaire, consult your doctor prior to physical activity.'. Read 2026-11-16 in a copy of the official form hosted by a municipal recreation department (the PAR-Q+ Collaboration's own site did not appear in search), through a summarizing fetch. The question wording here is the form's; the follow-up pages were not quoted, so the case does not reproduce them.

sources.cite: Riebe D, et al. Updating ACSM's recommendations for exercise preparticipation health screening. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2015 (November)
sources.note: Relevant text: the algorithm uses current physical activity, signs or symptoms and/or known cardiovascular, metabolic or renal disease, and desired intensity; not regularly active with signs or symptoms: 'Medical Clearance Recommended', then light-to-moderate exercise; regularly active and develops signs or symptoms: 'Discontinue Exercise and Seek Medical Clearance'. Read 2026-11-16 in a hosted copy of the paper's algorithm through a summarizing fetch; authors, volume and pages were not visible in that copy. The algorithm is the one ACSM's Guidelines carry; the 12th edition was not read.

sources.cite: ACSM Information On... Who Needs a Stress Test Before Exercising? (2017): warning signs 'Chest pain or pressure', 'Neck, jaw or arm pain', 'Shortness of breath', 'Unusual fatigue', 'Heart palpitations', 'Dizziness or a feeling like you are going to faint', 'Ankle swelling or overnight shortness of breath'; if they develop, 'discontinue exercise and seek a doctor's clearance right away'
sources.note: Read 2026-11-16 through a summarizing fetch. A consumer brochure; it does not say when to call emergency services, so the 911 step rests on the AHA page.

sources.cite: American Heart Association, Warning Signs of a Heart Attack: chest discomfort, discomfort in other areas of the upper body, shortness of breath, cold sweat, nausea, lightheadedness; 'Call 911 if you have any symptoms of heart attack'; 'Minutes matter'
sources.note: Read 2026-11-16 through a summarizing fetch; no review date was visible.

brief.situation: You are a personal trainer at a commercial gym. Marcus Hale, 52 (a fictional client), has booked a first session: he wants to lose weight and get fit before his daughter's wedding. He filled in the PAR-Q+ at the desk. You have an hour.
handover: The gym's emergency action plan: call 911, send the front desk to meet the crew, bring the AED.
Trainers screen, assess and program; diagnosing and medical advice are outside a trainer's scope.
howItWorks: Each task takes time: choose it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes.
The screen shows his PAR-Q+ answers, what you find, his read-outs and the rules that apply now.
When you end the session you write the record and explain your reasoning.

safetyNote: Teaching case for exam practice; fictional client. Not medical advice.

source.note: Three minutes of exertion before the chest tightness comes back is the author's figure, matching what the client says about the stairs.
Four more minutes of exertion with the tightness before it spreads and stops easing is the author's figure for teaching; real symptoms do not follow a schedule.
Three minutes of rest for the tightness to ease, as he describes on the stairs, is the author's figure.
Eight minutes for the ambulance is the author's figure; response times vary.

writeup.question: For the client record: what the screening found and why the form alone missed it, what you decided and on what basis, and what happens next.

parts.label: What the screen found
parts.criteria: Names the PAR-Q+ YES answers (blood pressure, medication) and the exertional chest tightness he did not count as 'pain' on question 2; says a conversation about exertion is what surfaced it.
parts.modelAnswer: PAR-Q+ YES to high blood pressure and its medication, follow-ups NO. Asked about stairs, he described chest tightness on exertion that eases with rest; he had answered NO to chest pain because he calls it tightness.

parts.label: Decision and basis
parts.criteria: Not regularly active plus a sign or symptom of cardiovascular disease: medical clearance before any fitness testing or training (ACSM algorithm; PAR-Q+ 'seek further information before ... a fitness appraisal'); no diagnosis or reassurance; during exercise a chest symptom means stop and call 911.
parts.modelAnswer: He is not regularly active and has a possible cardiac symptom, so ACSM recommends medical clearance before starting, and the PAR-Q+ says to seek further advice before a fitness appraisal. I did no exertional testing and did not guess at the cause.

parts.label: What happens next
parts.criteria: Clearance request with the PAR-Q+ and a note of the symptom, a plan to start after clearance at light-to-moderate intensity, and documentation.
parts.modelAnswer: He sees his doctor with the form and my note; we start at light-to-moderate intensity once cleared. Everything is in his record.

source.note: Exercise stopped within 2 minutes of a warning sign; a teaching figure, as for the physical therapy profile.

noProgress.rationale: Sending a client with an unevaluated exertional chest symptom away to start training on his own is never a safe outcome.

noReferral.narrative: He leaves with a program and an unexplained chest symptom no doctor knows about{isNull(symptomAskedAt) and isNull(symptomOnAt) ? ", one nobody asked him about" : ""}.

noCall.narrative: He had chest tightness during exertion and went home with a referral, but no one called 911 for a possible heart symptom.

"the reason he most needs clearance was never found" : reassured ? "you told him it was probably his fitness" : "the record is thin"}.

expertPath.text: Go through the PAR-Q+ and the follow-up questions; ask how active he is.
Ask what he notices on stairs and when he hurries: chest tightness that eases with rest.
No exertional testing. Explain why his doctor comes first, give him the PAR-Q+, the ePARmed-X+ and your note; set goals and a schedule for after clearance.

cleared.headline: Good: found, held, referred
cleared.body: The form said NO to chest pain; a question about the stairs said otherwise. Not regularly active with a possible cardiac symptom means medical clearance first, and nothing exertional today.

referredGaps.headline: Referred, with gaps
referredGaps.body: The referral is right, but the order or the words were not: ask about exertion before any test, keep to what he reports, and write it all down.

pushed.headline: A warning sign is a stop sign
pushed.body: Chest tightness during exercise means stop at once, sit him down and call 911. Encouraging him on turned a warning into an emergency.

noReferral.headline: The client left uncleared
noReferral.body: He is not regularly active and has a possible cardiac symptom (or nobody asked). ACSM recommends medical clearance before he starts.

noCall.headline: Chest discomfort during exertion: call 911
noCall.body: Stopping was right; the American Heart Association lists chest discomfort among the signs to call 911 for, and the gym's plan says so.

time_up.headline: No decision
time_up.body: The session ended with no plan and no record.

scoring.modelReasoning: PAR-Q+ YES to high blood pressure and medication; in conversation, exertional chest tightness he had not counted as pain. Not regularly active with a sign or symptom: medical clearance before testing or training (ACSM), and the PAR-Q+ says to seek further information before a fitness appraisal. No diagnosis or reassurance; a full record; start at light-to-moderate intensity after clearance.
